citation: Kim, Joochan, Jungryul Seo, and Teemu H. Laine. "Detecting Boredom from Eye Gaze and EEG." Biomedical Signal Processing and Control 46 (2018): 302-313. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bspc.2018.05.034.
discipline: biomedical signal processing / affective computing (HCI), designing and testing a dual-modality (EEG + eye-gaze) physiological boredom-detection method
thesis: Kim, Seo, and Laine identify a specific empirical gap: prior physiological boredom-detection studies examined EEG or eye-gaze signals in isolation, but none investigated whether the two correlate with one another when a person becomes bored. The authors design and run a short, single-session experiment (minimum protocol duration 120 seconds) in which participants view a deliberately monotonous, content-neutral video stimulus (a small circle slowly tracing a larger circle's outline for 90 seconds) while wearing a four-electrode consumer EEG headband (Muse) and a screen-based eye tracker (Eye Tribe), bracketed by a 30-second neutral baseline image and a post-stimulus 1-9 self-report boredom rating. Three hypotheses organize the study: (1) losing attention to the task signals boredom; (2) EEG and gaze data will each show a distinctive pattern, relative to an expected engaged state, when bored; (3) a correlation should therefore exist between EEG and gaze data during boredom. A non-machine-learning, threshold-based pipeline -- Signal Magnitude Area (SMA) thresholding for EEG and an Area-of-Interest hitbox/fixation-count algorithm for gaze -- identifies temporally coincident 'Potential Boredom Regions' (PBRs) across all 13 analyzed participants (of 17 recruited), while the self-report rating independently confirms boredom was elicited (mean 6.38/9) but does not itself correlate with any extracted physiological feature.

sections.title: Abstract and keywords
sections.summary: States the gap (no prior work links eye gaze and EEG in boredom), previews the video-stimulus experiment (N=13 analyzed), reports gaze-EEG correlations 'with all participants.'

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates emotion-aware computing (Picard's piano-tutor system; Chanel et al.'s boredom/anxiety/engagement game-adaptation scheme); argues boredom is comparatively neglected because it is a 'silent' emotion (Pekrun et al.) capable of both high and low arousal (Fahlman et al.); states three motivating reasons for choosing boredom and the three organizing hypotheses.

sections.title: 2. Background — 2.1 Emotion models
sections.summary: Wundt's three dimensions; Russell's 1980 Circumplex Model (Fig.1, arousal x valence); Grandjean et al.'s three-family taxonomy (dimensional, basic/discrete, componential-appraisal models).

sections.title: 2.2 Boredom (2.2.1 Defining, 2.2.2 Trait/state, 2.2.3 Attention)
sections.summary: Russell's quadrant-3 placement of boredom; Fahlman et al.'s aversive-unfulfilled-desire definition plus five manifestations; Eastwood et al.'s attention-based definition; trait vs. state boredom distinction (this study selects state); Fisher/Hamilton's attentional-failure account of boredom.

sections.title: 2.3 Detecting boredom / 2.4 Related work
sections.summary: Feidakis et al.'s psychological/physiological/behavioral taxonomy; Tables 1-3 (physiological data sources and types, analysis methods across seven prior studies, EEG brain-wave bands); detailed review of Shen et al.'s EEG-based SVM/kNN boredom classifier (67.1%/62.5% accuracy) and Jaques et al.'s eye-tracker-only classifier (SVM/Naive Bayes/Logistic Regression).

sections.title: 3.1 Experiment design
sections.summary: 3.1.1 stimulus/protocol (Fig.2 protocol; Fig.3 neutral image + video stimulus); 3.1.2 physiological data acquisition system (Table 4 supported sensors, Muse + Eye Tribe used); 3.1.3 participants/procedure (N=17 recruited, 9M/8F); 3.1.4 data analysis methods (Ogama heat maps + Table 5 parameters; SMA formula + individualized threshold formula).

sections.title: 3.2 Results
sections.summary: 3.2.1 physiological measurement (Figs.5-9; Algorithm 1 gaze-fixation-threshold detection; Table 6 fixation counts, all participants' PBR averages <17); 3.2.2 subjective measurement (Table 7 questionnaire, mean 6.38/9; no significant correlation with physiological features).

sections.title: 4. Discussion
sections.summary: Confirms all three hypotheses; discusses the null questionnaire-physiology correlation; the three anomalous participants (7,8,10); the algorithm's generalizability and limits; four named limitations (sample size, state-only design, post-hoc questionnaire timing, consumer-grade hardware).

sections.title: 5. Conclusion, acknowledgments, references
sections.summary: Restates contributions (gaze-EEG correlation finding, reusable video stimulus, generalizable fixation-threshold algorithm); funding (NRF-2015R1C1A1A02036469); 53 references.

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: explicitly adopted and operationalized as state boredom; the video stimulus is treated as an external factor, so 'we treat the boredom as a state rather than a trait'

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: background only (trait boredom, Boredom Proneness Scale, Farmer & Sundberg 1986); explicitly flagged as an unaddressed limitation and proposed future-work parameter

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: conceptual and experimental core; Eastwood et al.'s attention-based definition and Fisher/Hamilton's attentional-failure account ground Hypothesis 1; operationalized via gaze deviation from a defined AOI plus co-occurring EEG amplitude instability

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: engagement is the master term for what emotion-aware systems should preserve; 'engagement... is a prerequisite for reaching the flow state,' citing Csikszentmihalyi; Chanel et al.'s boredom/anxiety/engagement 3-class scheme

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: monotony built directly into the induction method (slow, generic circular-motion video, genre-neutral by design); credited in Discussion with eliciting boredom in all participants; meaninglessness not separately theorized

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: cited only, as one of Fahlman et al.'s five manifestations of boredom ('experiencing a slow passage of time'); not independently developed or measured

measures.label: gaze variance / fixation dispersion
measures.signal: binocular gaze position (x,y) and fixation points, sampled 30 fps
measures.apparatus: Eye Tribe eye tracker; heat maps and fixation analysis via Ogama v5 (fixations module, hitbox/AOI technique)
measures.treatment: 1-s-window hitbox technique around the moving-circle AOI (0.5 cm buffer = tracker's default error range), adapted from Eisenbarth & Alpers (2011)
measures.keyResult: 11/13 participants showed >=1 lost-focus heat-map region; every participant's average fixation count within EEG-flagged non-stable windows (PBRs) fell below 17, fixing 17 as the cross-participant gaze-based boredom threshold

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: single-item post-stimulus Likert-type boredom rating, 1 ('not boring at all') to 9 ('extremely boring')
measures.apparatus: on-screen questionnaire administered via the participant's display after video playback
measures.treatment: administered once, post-hoc (no continuous/time-stamped boredom indicator during viewing)
measures.keyResult: mean 6.38/9; authors characterize 11/13 (84.62%) as 'answered over 6' (score frequencies: 2->1, 3->1, 6->3, 7->4, 8->4); no significant correlation with any extracted EEG/gaze feature

measures.label: EEG alpha/theta power
measures.signal: background/cited only -- not Kim et al.'s own analysis
measures.apparatus: Table 3 documents delta/theta/alpha/beta band definitions generically; Shen et al. (2009) [24], cited related work, extracted alpha/beta/theta/delta/gamma power densities as SVM/kNN classifier features
measures.sampleN: n/a (cited study, not this paper's own sample)
measures.treatment: Kim et al. explicitly state they 'did not perform a detailed analysis of alpha, beta, theta and delta waves,' analyzing raw EEG amplitude via SMA instead
measures.keyResult: Shen et al.'s band-power SVM/kNN classifier achieved 67.1%/62.5% boredom-detection accuracy (background result, not Kim et al.'s own)

measures.label: pupil dilation / pupillometry
measures.apparatus: Table 4 lists 'eye gaze, pupil size' as an Eye Tribe-supported data type
measures.treatment: the reported gaze analysis (heat maps, AOI fixation counting) uses gaze position only; pupil size is never analyzed or reported in Results

measures.label: heart rate / HRV
measures.signal: background/cited only -- not part of this experiment's own instrumentation
measures.apparatus: Table 4 documents system support for a Microsoft Band wristband (heart rate, skin temperature), but it was not used in this experiment; Tables 1-2 review heart-rate/ECG/GSR use in other cited studies (Mandryk & Atkins 2007; Shen et al. 2009; Jang et al. 2015; Giakoumis et al. 2010/2011)
measures.keyResult: no own finding; background context only

measures.label: ML classification
measures.signal: background/cited + explicit future-work item -- not Kim et al.'s own analysis method
measures.apparatus: Table 2 surveys ML methods (SVM, kNN, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Neural Network, LDA/QDA/CART/SOM) across seven cited boredom/emotion-detection studies
measures.treatment: Kim et al.'s own method is explicitly non-ML (SMA + individualized statistical threshold + hitbox fixation counting); ML is deferred to future work ('we seek to utilize machine learning for in-depth data analysis')
measures.keyResult: Shen et al. 67.1% (SVM) / 62.5% (kNN) cited as comparison benchmarks; no ML result of Kim et al.'s own

readings.claim: Visual heat-map analysis (Ogama) found 11 of 13 analyzed participants showed at least one region of lost gaze focus relative to the moving-circle AOI during video playback, an initial confirmation of Hypothesis 1.

The EEG SMA-plus-individualized-threshold method classified 'stable' vs. 'non-stable' amplitude epochs per participant; cross-referencing non-stable epochs against gaze fixation counts via Algorithm 1 identified temporally coincident Potential Boredom Regions (PBRs) in all 13 analyzed participants, confirming Hypotheses 2 and 3.
Every participant's own average fixation count within their PBRs fell below 17, fixing 17 as a cross-participant gaze-based boredom-classification threshold for this specific video stimulus.

The post-stimulus questionnaire independently confirmed boredom was elicited (mean 6.38/9; 11/13 'answered over 6'), but no statistically significant correlation was found between questionnaire scores and any extracted physiological feature (SMA values; mean/SD fixation counts in PBRs and windows).

Three participants (7, 8, 10) had overall-session average fixation counts already below the derived threshold of 17, a limitation attributed to the fixation-count algorithm's insensitivity to fixation duration; despite this, all three showed EEG-gaze PBR correlations and the sample's highest subgroup mean questionnaire rating (7.7).

The gaze fixation-threshold detection algorithm generalizes to other single, well-defined-AOI stimuli, but does not straightforwardly extend to dynamic, multi-region stimuli where attention may legitimately shift among several valid targets.

The study names four limitations: small sample size (17, reduced to 13); a state-only design that disregards trait boredom; post-hoc-only questionnaire administration precluding fine-grained PBR verification; and consumer-grade rather than research-grade sensor hardware.

tensions.axis: boredom as necessarily low-arousal (Russell's Circumplex quadrant 3) vs. boredom as capable of high OR low arousal (Fahlman et al.)
tensions.note: Kim et al. explicitly flag this divergence: 'It is noteworthy that both Russell and Fahlman et al. incorporate the dimension of arousal in their definitions of boredom, but the only latter recognizes that a bored person can also exhibit high, agitated arousal.'

tensions.axis: rule-based/statistical thresholding (this paper's own method) vs. machine-learning classification (dominant in the reviewed related-work landscape)
tensions.note: Kim et al. use SMA + individualized mean/SD thresholding and hitbox fixation counting rather than any classifier, positioning this as a simpler first step and explicitly deferring ML methods (used by Shen et al., Jaques et al., and others) to future work.

tensions.axis: state-boredom operationalization (external, stimulus-induced, this paper's design choice) vs. trait-boredom measurement (individual disposition, Boredom Proneness Scale)
tensions.note: acknowledged as a deliberate scope restriction and later flagged as a limitation, since trait boredom 'may have an effect on threshold calculations for individual participants,' but not resolved within this study.

tensions.axis: physiological 'objectivity' vs. self-report 'subjectivity' as a convergent-validity problem
tensions.note: the paper's own null correlation between questionnaire scores and physiological/gaze features is a genuine internal tension the authors surface but do not resolve, proposing a control-vs-experiment-group design as a future remedy.

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- EEG channel
dataset_channels.note: Kim et al.'s 4-electrode consumer EEG apparatus (Muse; FP1/FP2/TP9/TP10; 220 Hz) and SMA-plus-individualized-threshold analysis offer a plausible methodological template for a future VR attention study's EEG channel, but a VR headset's integrated EEG (if any) would likely differ in electrode placement, sampling, and form factor from this screen-based, external-sensor setup; linkage requires the dataset entry's own instrumentation to be confirmed (P/anticipatory-application).

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- eye-tracking channel
dataset_channels.note: Kim et al.'s screen-based binocular eye tracker (Eye Tribe, 30 fps), Ogama heat-mapping, and AOI/hitbox fixation-count algorithm offer a plausible methodological template for a future VR attention study's eye-tracking channel, but VR headset-integrated eye tracking differs substantially in geometry (3D gaze vectors, headset-relative AOIs) from this study's 2D screen-based paradigm; linkage requires the dataset entry's own instrumentation to be confirmed (P/anticipatory-application).
